verses.text: The tax collectors kept coming to him. So did the people everyone called sinners.Whoever Jesus was — word had got around. They came to listen.

footnotes.content: "Tax collectors and sinners" was a fixed social category in Second Temple Judaism — not a moral diagnosis but a label for the people who had placed themselves, or been placed, outside the boundaries of covenant observance. Tax collectors (τελῶναι) collected local tolls under Roman-authorized contracts; they were despised both as cheats and as collaborators with the occupying empire. "Sinners" (ἁμαρτωλοί) was the broader category for anyone who failed to keep Torah in the ways that marked covenant membership — tithing, purity laws, Sabbath. Together they named the socially defined "lost," the people the three parables in this chapter are about to address. Hearing "sinners" as a piece of catechism vocabulary is exactly what the parables resist.

verses.text: And the Pharisees and the Torah scholars— the people who took the Law most seriously — muttered to one another: "This man welcomes sinners. He sits down and eats with them." That was the charge. Not that he taught them. That he ate with them.

footnotes.content: The Greek verb (διεγόγγυζον) is the same intensified compound the Greek Old Testament uses at Numbers 14:36, where the Israelites grumble against Moses after the spies' report — a muttering that represented a failure to trust God's surprising choices. Luke places these scribes and Pharisees inside a recognizable pattern: those who resist when God's people start being chosen in unexpected ways.

In the Jewish world of the first century, sharing a table was not a casual gesture. It was a covenant declaration. To eat with someone was to vouch for their standing — their purity, their place in the community, their acceptability before God. The verb (συνεσθίει, "eats together with") is the precise charge. It was not that Jesus taught sinners or was kind to them. He sat down at their table. That, in their categories, blurred the boundaries that defined who belonged to God's people and who did not.

verses.text: So he told them this story.
"Say one of you owns a hundred sheep and loses one. Doesn't he leave the ninety-nine out in the open country and go after the one that's lost — and keep going until he finds it?

footnotes.content: The Greek word (ἔρημος) is often translated "wilderness" or "desert" — but in Galilee it means open pastureland, the scrubby hillside grazing where flocks were normally kept. Shepherds worked cooperatively; leaving ninety-nine sheep there was not reckless abandonment but a realistic arrangement, since other shepherds remained with the larger flock. The parable's premise is plain and workable, not extravagant.

verses.text: And when he finds it, he lifts it onto his shoulders, already rejoicing.
He gets home and calls his friends and neighbors together: 'Rejoice with me. I have found my sheep — the one that was lost.'
I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who turns back than over ninety-nine upright people who don't think they need to."

footnotes.keyword: ninety-nine upright people who don't think they need to
footnotes.content: Who are the "ninety-nine righteous who need no repentance"? The phrase is almost certainly ironic. Jesus is speaking to Pharisees who count themselves among the upright. The irony cuts gently but cuts: if you think you need no turning, heaven has less joy over you than over the one who does. Notice too that the sheep in the parable never "repented" — it did not find its own way home; it was found and carried. The word "repentance" (μετάνοια, a turning) appears only in the application, not in the story.

What does it mean to say there is "joy in heaven" when one person turns back? For a modern reader, the idea that the heavens respond to events on earth is hard to take literally. The phrase works on two levels. In Jewish usage, "heaven" was a standard circumlocution for God — "joy in heaven" means "joy in God." The parallel at 15:10 makes it explicit: "joy before the angels of God." Jesus is claiming that the divine response to one human return is not cool approval or bureaucratic processing but celebration — extravagant, communal, excessive. Whether one reads this as metaphor for divine disposition or as cosmic event, the claim is unmistakable: what matters most to God is not who is kept out but who has been brought back.

verses.text: "Or a woman has ten silver coins— all her savings — and loses one. Doesn't she light a lamp, sweep the house, and search every corner until she finds it?

footnotes.content: A drachma was a Greek silver coin worth roughly a day's wages for a laborer. Ten drachmas were almost certainly this woman's dowry — the money she had brought into her marriage that remained, by law, hers. Losing one was losing a tenth of all her liquid savings. The typical village house of the period had rough stone floors with gaps between the slabs; coins fell into the crevices and stayed there. Archaeologists have found ancient coins in exactly these cracks at excavated sites.

verses.text: And when she finds it, she calls her friends and her neighbors together — the women she knows. 'Rejoice with me. I have found the coin I had lost.'

footnotes.content: Both Greek nouns here (τὰς φίλας καὶ γείτονας) are unambiguously feminine plural: "her women friends and her women neighbors." This is not a mixed gathering but a specifically female celebration circle. The detail is theologically loaded. The woman is placed as the exact structural parallel to the male shepherd of the previous parable — and her women's network mirrors his network of friends and neighbors. Together these two stories form Luke's most explicit male-female pairing: a shepherd and a woman, both as figures of God's searching love, both summoning their communities to celebrate. Heaven, in this parable, is a circle of women rejoicing.

verses.text: In the same way, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who turns back."
He went on: "A man had two sons.
The younger one said to his father: 'Father, give me my share of the estate.'As though the father were already dead. So he divided his property between them.

footnotes.keyword: Give me my share of the estate
footnotes.content: In first-century Palestinian culture, this request was devastating — in cultural terms the equivalent of openly wishing the father dead. Jewish inheritance law (Deuteronomy 21:17) permitted designation of assets before death but not distribution. By asking for his portion now, the son was saying: I want what I would get when you die, and I want it while you are still alive. The father had every legal and social right to refuse; he could have beaten the son, disinherited him, or publicly denounced him. His compliance — dividing his βίον, his "livelihood," the property that sustained the whole household — would have struck the audience as not merely generous but shocking.

verses.text: Not long after, the younger son turned everything he had into cash and set off for a country far away. There he ran through it all on reckless living.

footnotes.content: The Greek adverb (ἀσώτως) describes financial recklessness — wasteful, unbridled spending. It is not a euphemism for sexual immorality. The narrator deliberately does not say what the son did with his money. Later, the elder brother will accuse him of having spent it on prostitutes (15:30), but that is the elder brother's claim — the narrator never confirms it. The distinction matters more than it sounds. For centuries this "far country" has been weaponized in Christian moralism — most painfully, in our own day, in conversion-therapy frameworks that read it as code for queer identity. The text does not support that reading. The son's specific sin is left unspecified on purpose. The parable's claim is about welcome, not about cataloging anyone's particular shame.

verses.text: When he had spent everything, a hard famine settled on that country, and he began to be in want.
So he hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed pigs.

footnotes.content: For a Jewish listener, this detail was the absolute bottom. Pigs were profoundly impure under Torah (Leviticus 11:7–8; Deuteronomy 14:8). Feeding pigs meant not merely poverty but ritual defilement — sustained, daily contact with the animal most viscerally associated with Gentile impurity. The son is now as far from his covenant identity as it is possible for him to be.

verses.text: He would have filled his belly with the carob pods the pigs were eating; no one gave him anything.

footnotes.content: Carob pods (κεράτια) were standard livestock feed — edible by humans only in extremity, associated with destitution. A later Talmudic saying (b. Berakhot 63a) puts it plainly: "Israel turns back to God only when reduced to eating carob pods." Whether or not the audience knew that specific saying, the degradation was unmistakable: a son of Israel, envying the food of unclean animals.

verses.text: Then he came to his senses.What woke him was hunger. 'How many of my father's hired hands have bread to spare,' he said to himself, 'and here I am, dying of hunger.

footnotes.content: A classical Greek idiom (εἰς ἑαυτὸν ἐλθών, "having come to himself") for recovering right judgment after a period of distress or delusion — paralleled in Diodorus Siculus and Epictetus. It describes a cognitive return, not a religious experience. The son does not have a vision; he does a calculation. His father's hired workers eat better than he does. The turning starts in his stomach, not in his conscience — and the parable does not require it to be otherwise before the father responds.

The parable is unusually honest about what triggers the return: not remorse, not insight, not spiritual longing. Hunger. He came to his senses not through prayer but through pain. This unsentimental clarity is characteristic of how Jesus tells stories — crisis is allowed to be the door, and the door does not have to be pretty for the welcome on the other side to be real. So — what is your honest hunger, today? Not the dramatic version. The quiet, daily one. The tiredness that doesn't lift over the weekend. The relationship that has become performance. The job that pays well and starves something in you. The faith you no longer believe in but cannot quite leave. Hunger is not a failure of gratitude; it is information. It is the body and the soul telling you that the husks are no longer enough. Try just naming one such hunger this week — write it down, without trying to solve it. Naming is often the first move in a long return. The lineage on this is consoling: Ignatius taught that desolation is not the absence of God but often the precondition of clearer sight; twelve-step recovery builds its first step on something close to this verse's logic. The point is not to engineer a crisis. The point is that when one arrives unbidden, it is not a sign of failure. It can be the moment the father has already started running.

verses.text: I will get up and go to my father, and I will say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you.
I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me one of your hired hands.'

So he got up and went to his father. While he was still a long way off, his father saw him. Compassion seized him —the kind you feel in your body before your mind has caught up — and he ran and fell on his neck and kissed him.

footnotes.content: An older man of standing did not run in public in the ancient Mediterranean world. Running required pulling up one's outer garment and exposing one's legs — a loss of dignity for a man of his rank. Kenneth Bailey argued that the father may have been racing to reach his son before the village could enact a communal shaming ritual against the returning prodigal. Whether or not that specific reconstruction holds, the run is unambiguously a self-humbling: the father destroys his own honor to close the distance. He reaches his son before his son can reach him. The initiative — and the cost — are entirely his.

From σπλάγχνα — literally "intestines," "guts." The verb (ἐσπλαγχνίσθη) names compassion felt in the body before the mind has processed it: a gut-punch of love. The same word appears in the Greek Old Testament rendering of Jeremiah 31:20, where God says of wayward Ephraim, "my heart yearns for him; I will surely have mercy on him." Luke uses the word for Jesus and for God-figures in his parables (7:13; 10:33; 15:20). It is the signature emotion of the divine in his Gospel.

footnotes.keyword: fell on his neck and kissed him
footnotes.content: Three verbs in three beats: he ran, he fell on his neck, he kissed him. The accumulation is the point — the father does not pause to listen, to assess, to weigh the depth of the son's repentance. He is moving the whole time the son is rehearsing. Who has ever moved toward you like that — before you finished explaining yourself? A parent who pulled you into the house before the lecture could begin. A friend who interrupted your apology with food. A teacher who covered for you without making you watch them do it. These moments are formative in a way that organized teaching about love rarely is. They tend to rewire what you think is possible between human beings. This week, you could try being that person to someone — a colleague, a partner, a child you can sense is preparing to over-explain a small failure. Cut in early. Not to deny accountability; to disable the shame circuit before it locks. Henri Nouwen spent the last years of his life looking at Rembrandt's painting of this scene in the Hermitage and writing about what it cost to grow, finally, into the father. The cost is the same now. So is the freedom on the other side.

verses.text: The son said to him: 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son —' He never finished.

footnotes.keyword: I am no longer worthy to be called your son
footnotes.content: The son's rehearsed speech (15:18–19) ended with one more line: "Make me one of your hired hands." When the moment comes, that line never gets spoken. The best ancient manuscripts (P75, Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus) end the son's speech here; later copyists, troubled by the inconsistency, added the missing line to harmonize it with the rehearsal. The shorter text is almost certainly original — and the theological point is precisely this: the father interrupts. He does not wait for the petition to be completed. Grace acts before repentance is finished.

verses.text: The father was already speaking to his slaves: 'Quick. Bring the best robe and put it on him. A ring on his hand. Sandals on his feet.

footnotes.keyword: the best robe ... a ring ... sandals
footnotes.content: Each gift the father calls for is socially exact. The "best robe" (στολὴν τὴν πρώτην) was almost certainly the father's own finest garment — a visible, public act of status restoration in front of the whole household. The ring (δακτύλιον) was a signet ring: a legal instrument bearing the family seal and conferring authority to act in the family's name — not jewelry but the reinstatement of legal personhood. Sandals (ὑποδήματα) marked free persons; slaves went barefoot. By giving sandals, the father explicitly refuses the servant-status the son had proposed for himself. And the fattened calf (μόσχος σιτευτός, v. 23) was a grain-fed animal reserved for major celebrations — enough meat to feed a whole village. This is not a private family dinner. It is a public, community-wide feast: the father's declaration to the entire neighborhood that his son has been fully restored.

verses.text: Bring the fattened calf and slaughter it. Let us eat and celebrate.
For this son of mine was dead and is alive again. He was lost and is found.' And they began to celebrate.

footnotes.keyword: was dead and is alive again
footnotes.content: The Greek verb (ἀναζάω) means "to come back to life" — it is used elsewhere for literal resurrection. This is not metaphorical softness ("he was as good as dead"); it is deliberate resurrection language. The father's declaration echoes Ezekiel 37 — the valley of dry bones, where God tells exiled Israel: "I will put my Spirit in you, and you shall live." N.T. Wright reads this as the whole exile-and-return story in miniature: the son who went to the far country is Israel scattered among the nations; his return is the promised restoration; the feast is the celebration that exile is over. The same line returns, word for word, at v. 32.

verses.text: His elder son was out in the field. As he came near the house he heard music. Dancing.
He called one of the slaves over. 'What's going on?'
'Your brother is back,' the slave told him. 'Your father has slaughtered the fattened calf — because he has him home safe.'
He was furious. He would not go in. His father came outside and pleaded with him.

But he answered his father: 'Look. All these years I have slaved for you. I have never disobeyed one of your commands. And not once did you give me even a young goat, so I could celebrate with my friends.

footnotes.content: The Greek verb (δουλεύω) is the standard word for slave-labor — from δοῦλος, "slave." The elder son does not say "I have served you" or "I have worked for you"; he says "I have slaved." This is not simply a complaint about unfairness. It is a labor-exploitation complaint, and it tells us how he has experienced his years at home: not as joyful sonship but as forced obligation. And yet the father's answer in v. 31 does not dispute the years; he simply says, "you are always with me, and everything I have is yours." The elder son has had access to everything all along. He has been living as a hired hand inside his own father's house.

verses.text: But the moment this son of yours comes back — this one who has devoured your livelihood with prostitutes — for him you slaughter the fattened calf.'

footnotes.keyword: this son of yours ... with prostitutes
footnotes.content: Two details to hear carefully. First, "this son of yours" (ὁ υἱός σου οὗτος) — the elder brother refuses to say "my brother." The relational distancing is pointed, and the father will quietly correct it in v. 32 with "this brother of yours." Second, "with prostitutes" (μετὰ πορνῶν) — this is the elder son's accusation. The narrator never said the younger son spent money on prostitutes. The text at v. 13 used only ἀσώτως, a word for financial recklessness, not sexual behavior. The elder brother may be inferring, projecting, or repeating village gossip — but the narrator does not confirm it. Readers should not treat his claim as established fact.

verses.text: But the father said to him: 'My child, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours.

footnotes.content: The father uses τέκνον — "child," a tender vocative — not the formal υἱέ ("son"). In the face of the elder son's fury and contempt, the father reaches for the most intimate word available to him. The contrast between the elder son's clipped accusation and the father's quiet "my child" is the parable's emotional climax.

verses.text: But we had to celebrate and rejoice. Your brother was dead and is alive again. He was lost and is found.'"

footnotes.content: The father's "this brother of yours" (ὁ ἀδελφός σου οὗτος) directly corrects the elder son's "this son of yours" in v. 30. The father refuses the elder son's distancing and insists on the kinship: whatever the younger son has done, he is still your brother. The Greek joins two verbs of joy — εὐφρανθῆναι ("celebrate," the festive eating-and-drinking joy of a village feast) and χαρῆναι ("rejoice," the inner gladness named earlier in heaven's joy over the found). The father fuses both. And the small word ἔδει — "it was necessary," "it was fitting" — frames the feast not as a reward for behavior but as the only appropriate response to death becoming life.

The parable ends here. The elder son does not answer. We do not know whether he goes into the feast or stays outside. This silence is not a flaw of the text. It is the theological point. The Pharisees and Torah scholars who muttered at v. 2 are standing exactly where the elder son is standing — outside the celebration, with a legitimate complaint and an open invitation. The parable does not resolve their question for them. And — this needs naming clearly — the long Christian habit of reading the elder son as a figure for "the Jews" is a misreading. The father in this story is a Jewish man. The whole family is Jewish. The elder son is invited, not condemned, and the parable presents the invitation precisely so that no one — least of all the reader — can settle the matter on someone else's behalf. Every reader who has ever been faithful and resented someone else's welcome stands in the same place. The question is always the same: will you go in? Origen and the early church argued about whether the elder son was finally saved; the text refused to settle it for them. Karl Barth read the open ending as the gospel's deepest courtesy — God will not coerce anyone over the threshold. Dorothy Day, working in Catholic Worker houses, said the hardest part of hospitality was not the strangers but the people who came to help and could not stop comparing their service to others'. So this week: name one feast you have been standing outside of. Consider going in. Eat the food. Stay for one song. See what happens to the resentment when it cannot be fed by absence anymore.
